newsitem.title: GERMANY: Black Forest town offers currency union foretaste.
newsitem.headline: Black Forest town offers currency union foretaste.

text.p: Residents of this picturesque town in the hills of the Black Forest on Tuesday became the first Germans to get a foretaste of what life may be like if Europe's planned single currency becomes reality.
Under a two-week long experiment, the 20,000 citizens of Waldkirch and anyone who cares to visit can shop with specially issued euro coins as well as in their usual deutsche marks.
Some 50 businesses in the town took part in the scheme, coordinated by the local savings bank, by displaying prices in euros as well as marks.

In a cobble-stoned lane off the main street, one bakery with a European flag fluttering proudly outside was even advertising special offers for euro-spending shoppers. "Eight pretzels for four euros!" a poster proclaimed.

If European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) goes as planned, citizens in participating countries would face a similar situation between January and July 2002 as their national currency is phased out and the real euro is phased in.

Demand for the two special coins -- issued in denominations of three and 25 euros and exchanged at a rate of two marks to one euro -- was immense. At lunchtime, the bank had sold out of its stocks and was ordering more from a reserve.
But few people seemed willing to part with their euros, preferring to keep them as collectors' items or gifts.
"I've bought one for my uncle. He's from Waldkirch but doesn't live here any more so it'll be a nice souvenir for him," said 24-year old medical student Stefan Schoelzel.
Reporters from the Bonn press corps, who seemed to have invaded the sleepy settlement en masse, searched in vain for a morning shopper carrying out a genuine transaction in euros.
The closest they came was a woman buying some rolls but her purchase had been set up by a desperate television camera team.
"I think it's more of interest to collectors," said sales assistant Maria Burger in an electrical store. "I can't see the people here buying them at the bank and then just spending them again."
Waldkirch took its cue from its French twin town Selestat in the Alsace region which carried out a similar scheme in May.
The scheme has been timed to mark the 30th anniversary of Waldkirch's twinning with Selestat.

The coin is 40 mm in diameter, 10 mm wider than the three euro coin which has a silver centre surrounded by a golden rim. Both coins sport the coats of arms of Selestat and Waldkirch on one side and Waldkirch's castle on the other.

"A real discussion can only be provoked by tangible things. The issues themselves are very abstract, so schemes like this one are very helpful," said Dietrich Elcherlepp, the local member of the European parliament.
In the local Waldkircher Anzeiger weekly newspaper, the project was buried in the second section alongside results from local bowling clubs and a report on autumn fashion trends.
Residents seemed pleased with the scheme, the attention it has brought to their town and the boost to the local economy from an influx of journalists and coin collectors.
But some had reservations about monetary union itself.
"It may make sense but looking at things from an emotional point of view, I prefer my deutsche mark," said Helmut Disch, the co-owner of a hotel perched in woodland above the town.
